title: The Gupta Age

cards.b: The Guptas (c. 320 to 550 CE) are remembered for art, science and Sanskrit. Historians debate whether it was a golden age. Questions test rulers, sources and cultural achievements.

Founder: Sri Gupta; Chandragupta I (c. 319 to 335 CE) married the Lichchhavi princess Kumaradevi (Gupta era from 319 or 320 CE). Capital Pataliputra, later Ayodhya and Ujjain. Sources: coins, the Allahabad Pillar (Prayaga Prashasti), Fa-Hien’s travel account, Kalidasa, Vishakhadatta’s Devichandraguptam, Mehrauli iron pillar.

Called the “Napoleon of India” (V. A. Smith). The Prayaga Prashasti by Harishena records his conquests: Aryavarta (violent conquest), Dakshinapatha (captured and then freed: grahana-moksha-anugraha), forest tribes, frontier kings; foreign kings offered gifts. Performed Ashvamedha. Coins show him playing the veena. Patron of Vasubandhu; Sri Lankan king Meghavarna sent a mission.

Chandragupta II (Vikramaditya), c. 375 to 415 CE: defeated the Shakas of Western India (Rudrasimha III), gaining ports (Bharuch) and Ujjain; Navaratnas (Kalidasa, Amarasimha, Varahamihira); Fa-Hien visited. Kumaragupta I (c. 415 to 455): Nalanda founded. Skandagupta: repelled the Hunas; Sudarshana lake repaired. Later Guptas fell to the Huns (Toramana, Mihirakula) and regional rulers by about 550 CE.

Titles: Maharajadhiraja, Parameshvara. Provinces (bhuktis, under uparikas), districts (vishayas, under vishayapatis), villages (gramikas). Officers: Mahasandhivigrahika, Kumaramatya, Dandanayaka. A more decentralised pattern than the Mauryas: feudatories (samantas), land grants (agrahara), religious grants with administrative rights. Brahmin and temple lands grew. Fewer salaried officials, more land payment.

Fa-Hien noted safe roads and mild taxes. Gold coins (dinaras) in large numbers, but fewer silver and copper coins and a decline in long-distance trade in the later period (R. S. Sharma). Crafts: textiles, ivory, metallurgy (the Delhi Iron Pillar of Chandragupta II). Land grants and forced labour (vishti) increased. Towns declined according to some historians.

Literature: Kalidasa (Shakuntala, Meghaduta, Raghuvamsha), Shudraka, Vishakhadatta, Bharavi; Panchatantra; Puranas and Smritis (Narada, Brihaspati) compiled; Science: Aryabhata (Aryabhatiya, 499 CE; zero, decimal, the earth’s rotation, pi), Varahamihira (Brihat Samhita), Brahmagupta (later), Sushruta and Charaka (earlier works). Art: Deogarh Dashavatara temple, Sarnath Buddha, Ajanta, Udayagiri. Nalanda grew into a great university.

Nationalist historians (R. C. Majumdar, Altekar) called it a golden age. Marxist historians (R. S. Sharma, D. N. Jha) said it was the start of feudalism with landlordism, decline of trade and rise of untouchability (Fa-Hien’s mention of chandalas). Romila Thapar urges care with the term. Recent work stresses regional variety. The age had great art, science and literature but also growing social rigidity and worsening position of women (child marriage, restrictions in Smritis).

The Delhi Iron Pillar shows India’s early metallurgy; Aryabhata gave his name to India’s first satellite (1975). “Nalanda” inspired the new Nalanda University. Aryabhata’s zero and the decimal system are India’s contribution to global mathematics. Yet the golden age claim features in culture and history textbook debates.
